26.26.4.en: * It is a sign of God's tender love that He makes those who set snares fall into them, so that they cease from striving and from devising plots against their brethren.

26.27.0.en: St. John Chrysostom A lying tongue hateth those that are afflicted by it; and a flattering mouth worketh ruin [28].

26.27.1.en: He closes the chapter with a warning against the lying tongue that harms others and hates them, and likewise against the mouth that flatters another while the man plans the ruin and destruction of the one he speaks with. We may say that what the wise man aims at here is that we face the truth of our depths with complete frankness, and not cover what is in the heart of hatred and malice with a deceitful smile, or words of flattery, or lying and deceit.

26.27.2.en: * Lying is foreign to us, whether its subject is grave or slight, and even if someone lies with the intention of reaching some kind of good, this lie is nevertheless not commendable, for the Saviour says that lying comes from the evil one (Mt 5:37; Jn 8:44).

26.27.3.en: St. John of Asyut * Do not allow the spirit of lying to be found in you, lest the Lord deliver you to destruction.

26.27.4.en: * If you surrender your heart to him in false dreams, he grows more firmly rooted in vain thought, until he leads astray all who receive the spirit that loves the word of which it was written: "When he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own: for he is a liar, and the father of it" (Jn 14:8).

26.27.6.en: Gather me into the company of Your children!

26.27.7.en: * My heart rejoices in Your surpassing love.

26.27.8.en: You loved us and came down to us, to embrace all mankind in love, and to make all of them Your sons.

26.27.9.en: * Let me avoid the company of fools, who in their stubbornness persisted in resisting You!

26.27.10.en: I confess to You my ignorance, but You enlighten my depths with Your wisdom.

26.27.11.en: You give me understanding and wisdom, so that I desire nothing but to be in Your image, and to speak Your words!

26.27.12.en: No word of cursing will come out of my mouth, but only the words of blessing that are from You.

26.27.13.en: * Give me wisdom, that I may know when to speak and when to be silent.

26.27.14.en: Then I shall not go down with the stubborn fools, nor be provoked and bear the same marks as they.

26.27.15.en: But I shall walk in wisdom, and bear witness to You by Your work within me!

26.27.16.en: Let me avoid the company of the lazy, for in Your embrace I shall not know idleness.

26.27.17.en: You and the Father work for the sake of the whole world.

26.27.18.en: In Your love work in me and through me for the sake of Your Kingdom.

26.27.19.en: * Let me avoid the company of the stirrers-up of strife.

26.27.20.en: You came down to us to reconcile us with Your Father.

26.27.21.en: You gave us fellowship with the heavenly ones, You raised up from every tribe and people a holy people for Yourself; why then strife, when You are Peace itself.

26.27.22.en: O that I might possess You, and my heart be filled with peace; O that I might possess You, and the serpent not cast his malice into my mouth or my heart.

26.27.23.en: O that I might possess You, and my words be sanctified; I shall find no taste for gossip, no place in me for lying, and no need for the violent word.

26.27.24.en: Rather, let my words be salted with the salt of Your Holy Spirit!

27.0.0.en: Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth [1].

27.0.1.en: The past has gone by and will not return, and the future we do not know whether it will come upon us in this world or whether we shall pass away before it comes, but the moment we are living is ours. Through the present we benefit from the past, with its good things as well as our mistakes, and through it we work for the future, whether we are found in this world or the other. In this way we boast in the present day and sanctify it to the Lord, and live every moment of our life rejoicing.

27.0.2.en: By becoming accustomed to postponing to tomorrow, often the tomorrow in which we are to work never comes, because with every tomorrow we postpone to the tomorrow that follows it. Some say: "Postponing till tomorrow is a thief that steals a man's life."

27.0.3.en: The Holy Bible calls us not to postpone, especially concerning the salvation of our souls: "behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation" (2 Cor 6:2). "To day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts" (Heb 3:7-8). Felix the governor trembled when he heard Paul reason of righteousness, temperance and judgment to come, and instead of taking a decision to repent, he said: "Go thy way for this time; when I have a convenient season, I will call for thee" (Acts 24:25), and Felix did not get a convenient season to call for him until he died.

27.0.4.en: He who walks in the way of postponing to tomorrow will not reach a dwelling in which to settle.

27.0.5.en: * Let us not postpone to tomorrow, for we do not know what the next day may bring forth. And let us not say: "We shall overcome this habit little by little," for this thing will never come to an end. Therefore, to nullify this excuse, let us say: "If we do not amend the practice of swearing oaths today, we shall not postpone it to later, when countless matters press upon us. For we shall certainly die, and be punished, and lose all that we have. Let us not give Satan the benefit of our loitering, nor of the practice of delay," for if the Lord knows your soul to be fervent, He Himself also stretches out a hand of help to change your life.

27.0.6.en: St. John Chrysostom * Behold, the days are buried like the dead. Yesterday we buried yesterday, and behold, today we are advised that it will also profit. Weep then over yesterday which no longer exists, and raise your voice over today because it will pass as well. Behold, the days snatch you away, and life flees.

27.0.7.en: When the evening buries you, the morning raises you up.

27.0.8.en: It puts you to death daily so that you may know that you will die.

27.0.9.en: * The life of yesterday has fled from you, and behold, the life of today is swift to pass. Whether you are awake or asleep, the night does not stop on its course, and the day does not rest from completing its journey.

27.0.10.en: This life of yours is being plundered, so plunder from it the benefit.

27.0.11.en: Do not rely on the morning because it is bright, if your mind is not enlightened by God so that it may dawn.

27.0.12.en: Do not think that the evening is for rest, as long as your soul is tormented by the pains of evils.

27.0.13.en: * As you have driven repentance away with various excuses until now, awaken your will to drive away sin day after day, until victory meets you like wealth meets the poor man.

27.0.14.en: * Please God as you have pleased the world. Grow rich by poverty, as you grew poor by riches. Seek detachment as you sought possessions. Take your mind out of the world and direct it to God, as you took your soul out from God and behind the world.

27.0.15.en: * Until today you were not king of yourself, but a slave of the world. Be king of yourself, and serve it.

27.0.16.en: * If a thief robbed you, you would wail, while your life is being stolen from the life of God and you do not grieve over it. (Letter 43)

27.0.17.en: St. James of Serugh * Let us return to Him, beloved, and not postpone our amendment to the end of our life. Let us listen to the prophet who says: "Make no tarrying to turn to the Lord: and put not off from day to day" (Sir 5:7). For you "knowest not what a day may bring forth." Why do you postpone, O man, from day to day, when today may be your last day?

27.1.0.en: Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth; a stranger, and not thine own lips [2].

27.1.1.en: If a man is struck with the love of praise he loses the spirit of humility, and the grace of God forsakes him. Those who praise you may be sincere in their praise, but no man knoweth the things of a man, save the spirit of man which is in him (1 Cor 2:11). A man knows the truth of his weaknesses, stumblings and falls, and if God in His love covers him, then at least let him reject in his inner self the praise of men.

27.1.2.en: Many praise us today and blame us tomorrow, so he who is pleased by men's praise today loses his peace tomorrow.

27.1.3.en: * If I seem arrogant to you, it is because I bear witness to myself. For every man, when he wishes to bear witness to himself, seems haughty and proud; therefore it is written: "Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth."

27.1.4.en: St. Augustine * No one crowns himself, for this man who heaps praise on himself is rightly mocked, since it is written: "Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth; a stranger, and not thine own lips." But although hypocrites may remain undiscovered and receive honours from men, he says: "but God knoweth your hearts." For the Judge cannot be deceived; He sees the depths of our mind, and knows who is the true contender, and who steals by fraud the honour rightly due to another.

27.1.5.en: St. Cyril the Great * Our souls are a holy bride for the immortal Bridegroom, and the wedding is the divine Mysteries... So give heed to yourself, keeping your bridal chamber undefiled, and long to receive the heavenly Bridegroom, Christ the King, so that on the day of His coming He may make His abode in you with His Father, and you may have great praise before the angels and the holy archangels, and enter Paradise with great joy.

27.2.s.en: 3. Dealing with the wise and the fool

27.2.0.en: 3 A stone is heavy, and the sand weighty; but a fool's wrath is heavier than them both. 4 Wrath is cruel, and anger is outrageous; but who is able to stand before envy? 5 Open rebuke is better than secret love. 6 Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.

27.2.1.en: A stone is heavy, and the sand weighty; but a fool's wrath is heavier than them both [3].

27.2.2.en: The foolish or stupid man has no fear of the Lord in him, and does not walk in a spirit of godliness; if he is angry he loses his awareness, and acts with great violence without discrimination, so his wrath is heavier than stone and sand. Therefore it befits the wise man not to converse with him or confront him during his anger, but to keep silent and flee from his face. When Saul was angry with David without cause, the king lost his awareness, and called his son Jonathan, who loved David, "thou son of the perverse rebellious woman" (1 Sam 20:30), and could not bear to call David by his name, but called him "the son of Jesse," and "the son of death" (1 Sam 20:31), and determined to kill him by every means.

27.3.0.en: Wrath is cruel, and anger is outrageous; but who is able to stand before envy? [4]

27.3.1.en: The wise man warns us against the stealing of envy into our hearts, for although wrath is heavier than stone and sand, it is like a short-lived storm, and anger is also like a sweeping flood, that is, nothing can stand before it; but envy dwells in the heart and reigns over it, even if its outward manifestations disappear.

27.3.2.en: * The envious man does not count the disasters that befall him a trial; his trial is the good that befalls another, and conversely success for him is not that he should be happy but that trials should befall another. The envious man grieves to see the good works of men, and is glad at the disasters that befall them. It is said that the birds of prey that devour dead bodies are destroyed by a sweet smell (perfume), for their nature agrees with what is evil and corrupt. And anyone who falls under the control of this disease (envy) is destroyed by the happiness of his relatives and neighbours, but if he sees an evil trial he flies to it and puts his crooked beak into it and brings out the hidden disasters.

27.3.3.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa * Envy is hard to heal, because when its causes are sought it grows worse. It looks for external causes and not the inner truth, and its severity increases by rendering services and gifts to the envious man, because, as Solomon himself says: "he stands before the envious" (Prov 4:27). The more the other (the envied one) succeeds in submission and humility, or in the virtue of patience or generosity, the more the pricks of the other's envy increase, for he desires nothing but the destruction and death of the envied one.

27.3.4.en: Father Piamoun * Contentiousness and envy are born of vainglory, for if a man seeks the glory of men he bears a grudge against him who works and succeeds and is glorified, and envies him, and humility is the cure for that.

27.3.5.en: St. Abba Poemen * He who has found envy has found with it Satan, who brought it into being from of old.

27.4.0.en: St. Mar Isaac the Syrian Open rebuke is better than secret love [5].

27.4.1.en: If there is true love, the believer should care for the salvation of those he loves, and be frank with them. He criticizes them, but in a spirit of love without wounding their feelings. He shows them their faults, without exposing them.

27.4.2.en: * It is certainly clear that hidden sin contributes to the death of the sick person, for the sting of death is sin (1 Cor 15:56) as the Scripture says, and also: "Open rebuke is better than secret love." May no one hide a sin out of courtesy to another, lest the killing of the brother take the place of brotherly love.

27.4.3.en: St. Basil the Great * Rebuke is good, and is often better than silent friendship. Even if you think the friend himself has been hurt, rebuke him, and if the bitterness of correction wounds his mind, rebuke him and do not fear. For friendship must be sincere and steadfast in love.

27.4.4.en: St. Ambrose * We who were driven out from the original happiness of Paradise because of our boldness in desiring pleasures must return through bearing hardships with humility; we, the fugitives through our evil doing; there we did what is contrary to justice, here we suffer for the sake of justice.

27.4.5.en: St. Augustine * It befits us to rejoice when we are counted worthy of divine discipline.

27.4.6.en: Tertullian * If God disciplines those whom He loves, and He disciplines in order to correct, then it befits the brethren, especially the priests, not to hate but to love those who discipline them, so that they may correct them, for God foretold through Jeremiah, pointing to our present time, saying: [And I will give you pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with discipline] (cf. Jer 3:15).

27.5.0.en: St. Cyprian the Martyr Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful [6].

27.5.1.en: Wounds that come from a loving and wise heart, which knows what to rebuke and when and how far, these wounds are faithful and profitable. But he who wishes to win those around him, so he flatters them and takes part with them in their occasions without caring for their salvation, his conduct is counted as deceitful kisses in which there is neither faithfulness nor sincere love.

27.5.2.en: In perfect love the Apostle Paul differed with his friend St. Peter, and withstood him for the sake of the truth of the Gospel, as St. Barnabas also differed... but he bore hatred toward no one; rather the Apostle Paul's rule was pure love.

27.5.3.en: * Not everyone who forgives is a friend, nor everyone who strikes an enemy. For "Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful." Peter was wounded, and Judas kissed. But the kiss condemned Judas, for it carried the poison of betrayal, and the wound that Peter suffered was healed, for he washed his fault with tears.

27.5.4.en: St. Ambrose * When you rebuked me so that I should not tell the truth, did I not say to you: "I love you more than those who flatter you. In rebuking you I care for you more than all who show you respect?" Did I not also say to you: "Faithful are the wounds of friends rather than the deceitful kisses of enemies" (Prov 27:6). Had you yielded to my wounds, their kisses could not have led you to destruction, for my wounds work for your healing, but their kisses push you to a disease hard to cure.

27.5.5.en: St. John Chrysostom * Who is this friend whose wounds are better than the kisses of an enemy? The answer is clear to anyone who knows the mystery of salvation. For the true, steadfast friend does not cease to love us even while we are still enemies, but the enemy (the devil) is treacherous and violent. He subjects us to death though we have not harmed him.

27.6.0.en: 7 The full soul loatheth an honeycomb; but to the hungry soul every bitter thing is sweet. 8 As a bird that wandereth from her nest, so is a man that wandereth from his place. 9 Ointment and perfume rejoice the heart: so doth the sweetness of a man's friend by hearty counsel.

27.6.1.en: The full soul loatheth an honeycomb; but to the hungry soul every bitter thing is sweet [7].

27.6.2.en: Great hunger opens a man's appetite for food, and gives him an enjoyment and taste of it which he does not find when he is full.

27.6.3.en: People's indulgence in various kinds of food has made them lose their taste for food, so many try to be inventive in kinds of food, in order to attract the man of today to food, even if it is not healthy for them.

27.6.4.en: When we feel hunger for the word of God as food for the soul, we eat it and ruminate on it and meditate on it with delight. Perhaps the wise Solomon wishes to bring out the practical truth that the rich man, with his huge wealth and sumptuous foods, is not as happy as the poor man eating simple food, for he finds delight in it. The rich man often finds bitterness or unhappiness in what is sweet, while the poor man finds sweetness in what seems bitter!

27.6.5.en: * For although the telling of holy matters is often repeated, the mind that feels a thirst for true knowledge is never disgusted by its fullness, but every day receives the word as something new that it needs. In any case it often listens to it with great eagerness, and speaks of it. And repetition, for him, confirms him without weariness in the knowledge he already has.

27.6.6.en: This is the sign by which a mind is known to be cold and arrogant, that it receives the remedies of the words of salvation with contempt and carelessness, although they are offered with zeal and great earnestness, and that is because "the full soul loatheth an honeycomb; but to the hungry soul every bitter thing is sweet" (Prov 7:27).

27.6.7.en: So if these things are taken with care, and stored up within the soul, and sealed with the seal of stillness, they become like wine sweet to the taste, which gladdens the heart of man, and are aged by being stored long in the thought with steadfast patience, and a delightful fragrance comes out of the vessel of the heart, and it becomes a perpetual spring that overflows with the depths of experience in abundance, and is like watered channels. Virtue pours out abundant streams as from the deep well of your heart.

27.6.8.en: Father Nestor * Do not let the delights of the rich, by worldly measures, entice you, as though they were something useful. They delight in the art of cookery for their pleasure; but you women, surpass their excessive foods by fasting and moderation in eating, for the Scripture says: "The full soul loatheth an honeycomb" (Prov 27:7).

27.6.9.en: * Do not be deceived by the delights of the world's wealth, as though it contained something useful for vain pleasure. The worldly esteem the art of cookery, but you surpass their abundance of food with fasting and cheap food. It is written: "The full soul loatheth an honeycomb" (Prov 27:7). Do not be filled with bread, and you will not desire wine.

27.7.0.en: St. Syncletica As a bird that wandereth from her nest, so is a man that wandereth from his place [8].

27.7.1.en: The pure man is marked by a spirit of contentment and a life of thanksgiving, and so feels a kind of satisfaction and stability despite his struggle and striving and continual progress and growth in everything. But the unbeliever is not satisfied even if the whole earth is given to him, and will not rest, and feels no stability, for he is always murmuring. He is like a bird that forsakes its nest, and so is exposed to dangers.

27.7.2.en: The Apostle says: "But the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal" (1 Cor 12:7). "But now hath God set the members every one of them in the body, as it hath pleased him" (1 Cor 12:18). Therefore it befits the believer to recognize the gift that has been given him by God, and to kindle it with joy and faithfulness, without boasting over one who does not have the same gift, and without envying one who he thinks has a higher and greater gift than his own.

27.7.3.en: What is the nest that the bird leaves and so goes astray, but the embrace of God opened to us through the Cross, to which His Holy Spirit carries us, and in which we settle in a spirit of exultation? Demas left this nest, of whom the Apostle Paul said: "For Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world" (2 Tim 4:10).

27.7.4.en: The man sanctified to the Lord lives in this world as in heaven, and because of him peace comes upon those around him.

27.7.5.en: * Blessed is the city of Alexandria, of which you are the patrons! And the cities of Sodom would not have perished and turned to ashes if ten righteous had lived in them, and the other cities would not have been overturned if they had kept among them such holiness as yours. And the Holy Bible tells how the friends of the most godly Job, who were the objects of wrath (from God), were saved by his merit: "My servant Job shall pray for you: for him will I accept: lest I deal with you after your folly" (Job 42:8).

27.7.6.en: * What virtues adorn your lives, so dear to God! What a bright crown these virtues make! How great with you is perseverance in good works! The peace that reigns over you is by virtue of your distance from vices, and of the humility which is the sign that Christ reigns over you, which Satan lost from the beginning.

27.7.7.en: It was my bounden duty to write to you and tell you this, since it is written: "The memory of the just is blessed" (Prov 10:7), and the praise of the righteous gladdens the people (see Prov 29:2). So when some remember you, it is natural for them to incline to praise you.

27.7.8.en: St. Abba Serapion, Bishop of Thmuis * Hate your belly and the needs of this world and evil desires and honours, as though you did not yet exist in this world, and you will acquire peace.

27.7.9.en: St. Abba Anthony the Great * May the peace that comes from the Lord overflow in you beyond all measure, that heavenly peace that raised the light above the world. That which the prophets proclaimed and of which the righteous spoke, and which the angels announced with glad tidings. It is the peace that the Lady the Virgin Mary received and bore the Saviour of the world, that which came upon the dead, which split the rocks, opened the tombs, and gave life back to the dead, set free the captives and loosed the bound and enslaved, and tore up the bond of Adam's condemnation, and engraved a heavenly law in souls, and joined divinity to humanity, setting creation free, and killed sin, lifting the curse from the earth, breaking down the barrier of enmity, raising from the dust the body of Adam, whom He had condemned and then brought into the Paradise of the promise, and made him walk in newness of life, he who knew nothing but death. And that we might become His brethren He made us also to be born of His Father.

27.8.0.en: St. Abba Macarius Ointment and perfume rejoice the heart: so doth the sweetness of a man's friend by hearty counsel [9].

27.8.1.en: As sweet scents and incense bring joy to the heart of man, so the counsel of a sincere friend carries a special sweetness. And as perfumes refresh the senses of the body and stir in it a kind of vitality and energy, so the counsel of a sincere friend supports a man and increases the friendship between them. The prophet David found in Jonathan the son of Saul a sweet friend (2 Sam 1:26).

27.8.2.en: This proverb calls us to attach ourselves to sincere friends, especially old friends at the level of the family. There is no gift so precious as offering wisdom to a friend upright in heart.

27.8.3.en: * A person may not have bread to give in alms to the needy, but what is greater is to have a tongue able to give. For refreshing the mind, which lives for ever, with the food of the word, is more important than refreshing the stomach of the body, which will die, with earthly food.

27.8.4.en: Caesarius, Bishop of Arles * Look for the strength of the leader in his wisdom more than in the size of the divisions of his army...

27.8.5.en: If a city has many mighty men but they lack wisdom, these are unable to support it (Eccl 7:19).

27.8.6.en: The spiritual interpretation (of the phrase) is that the world is called a city, that is, the world that surrounds us.

27.8.7.en: No one can live without harm unless divine wisdom has been given him.

27.8.8.en: If wisdom does not help, those in authority (the mighty) can do nothing, whether you mean angels or saints.

27.8.9.en: If wisdom does not support, the city will not be saved.

27.8.10.en: One can see the soul of every human being as a city. Even if someone has a thousand earthly thoughts to help a city, they cannot support him unless wisdom comes down, and issues a command and supports him.

27.9.0.en: Thine own friend, and thy father's friend, forsake not; neither go into thy brother's house in the day of thy calamity:

27.9.1.en: for better is a neighbour that is near than a brother far off [10].

27.9.2.en: When a trouble comes upon a man, it is better for him to have recourse to his neighbour who is sincere toward him, his friend and the friend of the family, than to rely on kinship alone and have recourse to his brother who is far away. Here his call is to cleave to the neighbour as a true personal friend and at the level of the family.

27.9.3.en: * Solomon says: "Better is a neighbour that is near than a brother far off." Therefore a person in general relies on the good will of a friend more than on the ties of kinship with his brother. For good will prevails by far more than the guarantees given through nature.

27.10.0.en: My son, be wise, and make my heart glad, that I may answer him that reproacheth me [11].

27.10.1.en: The wise Solomon feels his fatherhood toward the one he speaks to or teaches. Nothing so gladdens the father's heart as that his son be wise according to the Spirit, so that he glories in him. But if the son rejects wisdom and walks in folly, the father feels as one in disgrace and shame.

27.10.2.en: * A person's wisdom makes his face shine, but not the face of the body, not a member of the flesh, but the inner face of the person... The inner face of man shines with wisdom. But wisdom, light, the Logos, truth, and other concepts are alike, for they apply to Christ.

27.10.3.en: St. Didymus the Blind * Let us imitate this man (Job), who put his adversaries to shame by his silence! He truly showed the strength of his spirit, for the insults did not affect it. And he openly showed the purity of his conscience, for he did not yield to the accusations, but made light of them, as though they were a reproach not directed against us.

27.10.4.en: But we want to be justified... and when the desire for revenge masters us, we proclaim it. For the Holy Scripture says: "Put away the insult from thee" (Prov 11:27) LXX, and take off thy cloak from thee, for a harmful man passes by (cf. Prov 13:27) LXX. Therefore let us be silent until he passes by and is not provoked, lest he burn our garment. For it is written: "Kindle not the coals of a sinner, lest thou be burned with the flame of his fire" (Sir 8:10).

27.10.5.en: For this reason the righteous man is silent, even if a servant has wronged him.

27.10.6.en: Even if a poor man insults him, the righteous man is silent, even if a sinner rebukes him, the righteous man laughs, even if a weak man curses him, the righteous man blesses...

27.10.7.en: David was silent when Shimei the son of Gera cursed him (cf. 2 Sam 5:16-14). And Job laughed (cf. Job 6:19) LXX. And Paul blessed, for he says: "being reviled, we bless" (1 Cor 12:4)...

27.10.8.en: And what Christ said in words He also fulfilled in deed and example. For when He was on the Cross, He said of His persecutors who were wronging Him: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do" (Lk 34:24). And He prayed for those who wronged Him, although He Himself could forgive them their wrongs!

27.11.0.en: A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself;

27.11.1.en: but the simple pass on, and are punished [12].

27.11.2.en: This proverb came corresponding to what is found in (Prov 22:3). For the wise man, seeing the storm of evil coming, takes care not to waste his time and energies in facing it, but wisely hides himself until it passes. But the foolish think they can face it, and so waste their time and shatter their energies for no profit.

27.12.0.en: 13 Take his garment that is surety for a stranger, and take a pledge of him for strangers. 14 He that blesseth his friend with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, it shall be counted a curse to him.

27.12.1.en: Take his garment that is surety for a stranger, and take a pledge of him for strangers [13].

27.12.2.en: It corresponds to the proverb in Proverbs 20:16, where the wise man urges us not to be rash, going surety for a stranger whom we do not know and whose means we do not know, lest we be compelled even to pledge our garment.

27.13.0.en: He that blesseth his friend with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, it shall be counted a curse to him [14].

27.13.1.en: He who does not consider his neighbour's rest, and praises him with a loud voice early in the morning, depriving him of his rest, his praise is counted a curse. And this conduct of his reveals his insincerity or his failure to perceive his neighbour's needs.

27.13.2.en: He who overdoes the praise of his friend in truth deceives him, and carries no spirit of sincerity and faithfulness toward him.

27.13.3.en: When Absalom praised every man who had a suit and came to David the king, saying to him: "See, thy matters are good and right; but there is no man deputed of the king to hear thee" (2 Sam 15:3), and he refused to let anyone bow down to him, but put forth his hand and took him and kissed him, Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel. In all this Absalom was a deceiver.

27.14.0.en: 15 A continual dropping in a very rainy day and a contentious woman are alike. 16 Whosoever hideth her hideth the wind, and his right hand grasps oil.

27.14.1.en: A continual dropping in a very rainy day and a contentious woman are alike [15].

27.14.2.en: When rain falls on the roofs of houses without ceasing, and the water seeps from the roofs into the rooms, the sound of the rain becomes extremely disturbing and does not subside; so the contentious, talkative woman does not rest and does not leave the household in peace by day or night.

27.14.3.en: * If the timbers that support the roof are thin and weak, and the owner of the house is negligent and does not look after the building, the roof will not keep the rain from seeping into the house. And this causes the roof timbers, which cannot bear the weight of the rain falling on it, to bend, and then the weak wooden pillars, which cannot bear the extra weight, break, and the water gathered on the bent roof penetrates into the house. So the rain drives the man out of his house when its flow increases, as it is said in the Book of Proverbs (Prov 27:15). Therefore the symbols in the proverb (Eccl 10:18) encourage us to be firm against the assaults of the passions, so that we do not bend under their weight, and the water enter our hearts and spoil all the treasures stored there.

27.15.0.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa Whosoever hideth her hideth the wind, and his right hand grasps oil [16].

27.15.1.en: When the family tries to hide the fact that strife rules it, without treating it, it is like one who tries to hide the wind in his hand, and prevent its blowing, or to grasp oil and hold it.

27.15.2.en: * Do you observe a soul trained in virtue? It receives with pleasure the accusations of the righteous against it, while it rejects the chatter of the wicked.

27.15.3.en: St. John Chrysostom St. Gregory of Nyssa gives us an interpretation of this wind, for he sees the bride, the queen, that is, the holy human soul, commanding the north wind, which signifies the evil passions arising from the powers of darkness, to awake and depart from her, while she asks the south wind to blow upon her.

27.16.0.en: 17 Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend. 18 Whoso keepeth the fig tree shall eat the fruit thereof: so he that waiteth on his master shall be honoured. 19 As in water face answereth to face, so the heart of man to man. 20 Hell and destruction are never full; so the eyes of man are never satisfied. 21 As the fining pot for silver, and the furnace for gold; so is a man to his praise. 22 Though thou shouldest bray a fool in a mortar among wheat with a pestle, yet will not his foolishness depart from him. 23 Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks, and look well to thy herds. 24 For riches are not for ever: and doth the crown endure to every generation? 25 The hay appeareth, and the tender grass sheweth itself, and herbs of the mountains are gathered. 26 The lambs are for thy clothing, and the goats are the price of the field. 27 And thou shalt have goats' milk enough for thy food, for the food of thy household, and for the maintenance for thy maidens.

27.16.1.en: Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend [17].

27.16.2.en: Iron is polished by rubbing against iron, as an iron knife is rubbed against an iron file, and the knife becomes sharp. So it befits a man, by friendly contact with his brother and exchange of thoughts with him, to be supported and encouraged. But he who withdraws from people and takes counsel with no other remains narrow in thought, poor in resource, shut up around himself, greedy. This contact, or what we call communal fellowship, benefits us in every aspect of our life, whether practical, social, economic or spiritual. The spiritual man benefits spiritually from his brother, and benefits him.

27.16.3.en: * Formerly we did not receive into our dwelling anyone of another race and with customs different from ours, but now, after the coming of Christ, we live together in fellowship with them.

27.16.4.en: St. Justin * Everyone must use fully all that he has for the common good. If you have wisdom or strength or wealth or anything else, let it not be for the ruin of your fellow servants nor for your own ruin.

27.16.5.en: Where does the great disparity in the conditions of life come from? From the greed and arrogance of the rich.

27.16.6.en: St. John Chrysostom * As the great river flows in thousands of channels through a fertile land, so let your wealth run through many channels into the houses of the poor. Wells from which water is drawn overflow with what is better; but those left unused spoil. So money, if it is kept, becomes worthless, but if it moves and passes from hand to hand, it helps society and increases.

27.17.0.en: St. Basil the Great Whoso keepeth the fig tree shall eat the fruit thereof: so he that waiteth on his master shall be honoured [18].

27.17.1.en: He who guards the fig tree and takes care of it has the right to eat of its fruit. And he who keeps his master's word, and is careful of his commandment, and works in a vineyard, will surely receive a reward for his faithfulness to his master; every watching or diligence of his has its reward, even for the servant in his dealing with his master.

27.17.2.en: The Lord Christ says: "If any man serve me, let him follow me; and where I am, there shall also my servant be" (Jn 12:26). And the Apostle Paul says: "The husbandman that laboureth must be first partaker of the fruits" (2 Tim 2:6).

27.17.3.en: * Paul tells his hearers not to be slack merely because God seeks them out and sends them as ambassadors. On the contrary, for that very reason we must please Him and reap our spiritual blessings.

27.18.0.en: St. John Chrysostom As in water face answereth to face, so the heart of man to man [19].

27.18.1.en: The face of clear water is counted the oldest primitive mirror; a man looks at the water and sees the image exactly like his own face. So, since the heart of man is corrupted, and sin has struck all the hearts of men, he who wishes to know his brother's heart contemplates it and perceives the truth of human weakness, and knows that the heart of man is "deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked" (Jer 17:9). And all need a Saviour.

27.18.2.en: * By the previous parable the lost sheep pointed to the family on earth, for we know that we belong to God, the God of all, who creates things out of nothing, and as it is written: "It is he that hath made us, and not we ourselves" (Ps 100:3), and also: "For he is our God; and we are the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand" (Ps 95:7). And by this second parable, in which he compares the lost one to a drachma, and that it is one of ten, that is, of a perfect number... it is evident that we bear the royal likeness and the royal image of the God of all, for the drachma, I think, is stamped with the royal likeness. So if we had fallen and become lost, we found Christ, and He formed us in holiness and righteousness after His image, a matter that no one doubts, since the blessed Paul wrote thus: "But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord" (2 Cor 3:18). And he sent to the Galatians these words: "My little children, of whom I travail in birth again until Christ be formed in you" (Gal 4:19).

27.18.3.en: The search was made for what had fallen, and the woman lit the lamp, and as I said, we were found by the wisdom of God the Father, who is the Son, when He shone upon us with His divine, intellectual light, and the sun arose, and the day dawned and the day star arose (2 Pet 1:19) as the Scripture says. God also said in another place through one of the holy prophets about Christ the Saviour of us all: "My righteousness draws near swiftly, and my mercy will be revealed, and my salvation will burn like a lamp" [(Isa 62:1) the Septuagint]. As the Lord also said of Himself: "I am the light of the world" (Jn 8:12), and said: "I am come a light into the world, that whosoever believeth on me should not abide in darkness" (Jn 12:46). So by the light that which was lost was saved, and became a joy to the powers above.

27.19.0.en: St. Cyril the Great Hell and destruction are never full; so the eyes of man are never satisfied [20].

27.19.1.en: Most people long to make journeys around the world, because their eyes are not satisfied with what they see. And now that the world has become small in man's eyes he wishes to set out for the planets.

27.19.2.en: The eyes of man are satisfied only by the heavenly Bridegroom, who is without limit. He alone fills the emptiness of the heart and satisfies the eyes.

27.19.3.en: He likens the eyes of man to Hades and destruction, which are not satisfied by people entering them, for the place of the dead keeps on swallowing the newcomers among human beings who thought that the world could satisfy them and give them happiness, but the world casts them into Hades and destruction.

27.19.4.en: * This is the essence of Christianity: the proclamation of the person of our Lord Jesus, the self-giving Love, and receiving Him as a paradise for the soul; therefore He cried, saying: "If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink," "whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely."

27.19.5.en: And so, when the soul needs to know the way, walking amid the sweeping currents of the world and the misleading lusts of the flesh, she sees her Beloved offering Himself as a ladder by which she ascends to heaven, her final homeland, and He says to her: "I am the way, the truth" (Jn 14:6).

27.19.6.en: And when she needs food to sustain her, by which she grows and lives, she sees in her Beloved all satisfaction and the source of her life, longing for her to accept to eat Him and live by Him, as He assures her: "I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst" (Jn 6:35).

27.19.7.en: And when she feels the delights of the world and its pleasures and cares and burdens, the lusts of the flesh and its passions, and the war of Satan and his deceptions, He declares to her: "I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live" (Jn 11:25).

27.19.8.en: And when she feels the need of a leader who supports and shepherds her, He reveals to her: "I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep" (Jn 20:11).

27.19.9.en: And when she feels an emptiness within her, she longs for a friend, self-giving, disinterested, gentle, longsuffering, and a bridegroom who listens to her secrets, whom she converses with and who converses with her; He presents Himself to her as a friend of sinners and tax collectors, and a bridegroom to those who believe in Him.

27.19.10.en: This is the Paradise that never dries up, and overflows without limit, gives satisfaction as much as we receive, and entreats everyone to receive Him, imploring: "Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man open to me, I will come in to him, and will sup with him," and if he does not open to me, I knock again and again, in the hope that his heart will soften and open to me, because I love him!

27.19.11.en: He came incarnate, to restore to the soul its happiness and fill its corners, and remove anxiety from it.

27.19.12.en: O my poor soul, what are you seeking?!

27.19.13.en: If you want wisdom, you will find Jesus the source and spring of wisdom, indeed He is Wisdom Himself!

27.19.14.en: And if you seek strength and power, He is the Almighty!

27.19.15.en: If you search for pleasure and delight, He is the spring of true joy!

27.19.16.en: If you long for intoxication, His love intoxicates the soul!

27.19.17.en: If you hunger for bread, He is the bread of life!

27.19.18.en: And if you are eager for riches, He is the Creator of all!

27.19.19.en: And if you want rest, you will find your rest in Him alone...! Receive Him, for you have no other who can satisfy you.

27.20.0.en: St. Augustine As the fining pot for silver, and the furnace for gold; so is a man to his praise [21].

27.20.1.en: Nothing reveals the dross in gold and silver like the fire of the crucible, and nothing exposes and tests a man like the fire of men's praise of him. For it is easy for a man to bear an insult without harm, but to bear the praise of men without falling into pride and self-esteem is extremely hard. It is said in The Garden of the Monks: "He who cannot bear a word of insult, how can he bear a word of praise?!"

27.20.2.en: The conceited man is not satisfied with praise, but asks for more without ceasing, and the weak man believes the word of praise, and the strong man ignores the word of praise and counts it as though it had not been!

27.21.0.en: Though thou shouldest bray a fool in a mortar among wheat with a pestle, yet will not his foolishness depart from him [22].

27.21.1.en: As the husks that cling to wheat are not removed by grinding it in a mortar, so evil is not removed from the fool who persists in his folly from his childhood (Prov 22:15) without any desire to repent.
